title: Who Holds Sovereign Debt and Why It Matters
summary: BIS Working Paper No. 1099 examines investor composition in sovereign debt markets across 95 countries over 1991-2018 (1744 country-year observations). The paper finds that non-bank private investors absorb a disproportionate share of sovereign debt increases, accounting for 69% of new debt while holding only 46% on average. Counterfactual analysis shows emerging market sovereigns face a 10% increase in debt costs by 6.7%, but would face a 9% increase if non-bank investors were absent, indicating these economies are particularly vulnerable to shifts in non-bank investor demand.
key_points: Non-bank private investors absorb 69% of new sovereign debt increases while holding only 46% of outstanding debt on average
For foreign-held debt, non-banks account for 75% of the increase despite comprising only 42% of foreign holdings
Private banks absorb less than proportional to their holdings: 20% of new debt vs. 28% average holdings
Aggregate government debt-to-GDP has reached historical highs post-Covid for both advanced and emerging economies
Emerging markets with higher EM debt face 6.7% cost increase per 10% debt increase, rising to 9% without non-bank participation
Investor base composition differs markedly: domestic share declining for AEs while increasing for EMs
why_it_matters: Understanding who holds sovereign debt is critical for governments managing refinancing risk and borrowing costs. The findings suggest non-bank investors (investment funds, pensions, insurance companies) are the marginal price-setters in sovereign markets, meaning their demand dynamics drive funding costs. Emerging market governments are particularly exposed to shifts in non-bank sentiment, as losing this investor base would significantly raise their cost of capital.
macro_context: The paper documents structural changes in sovereign debt investor composition globally, with implications for fiscal sustainability. Non-banks' higher responsiveness to yields creates a self-reinforcing dynamic: as debt rises, these investors absorb supply but demand a higher yield premium, particularly in emerging markets. This has direct implications for fiscal policy constrained by debt sustainability thresholds.
market_structure_context: The paper provides granular data on the investor base decomposition: domestic vs. foreign, and within foreign: private banks, private non-banks, and official creditors (central banks, IMF, World Bank). This decomposition is essential for understanding sovereign bond market liquidity, price discovery, and potential bid-ask dynamics during stress periods when investor composition shifts.
important_numbers: 69% of new debt absorbed by non-banks
75% of foreign debt increase from non-banks
20% of new debt absorbed by banks
